lessons.title: Meet the devices you already use

sections.title: Devices you may already have

blocks.html:
A digital device is a tool that stores and shares information. Canada’s Skills for Success describe Digital as the ability to use digital technology and tools to find, manage, apply, create, and share information and content. One official component is using digital devices, including computers, tablets, smartphones, and other handheld devices. Another is knowing basic words that most devices share, and using basic functions that are common to most of them.

You may already use more than one of these:

  • A desktop computer usually stays on a desk. It often has a separate screen, keyboard, and mouse.
  • A laptop is a portable computer with a built-in screen and keyboard.
  • A tablet is a flat screen you control mostly by touch.
  • A smartphone is a phone that also works like a small computer.

Get Cyber Safe calls mobile devices today’s multi-tools. People use them as cameras, maps, payment tools, watches, and more — and sometimes to make phone calls. That extra usefulness also means a phone can hold photos, messages, and other personal information. You do not need every device to start. Many libraries and adult learning centres have computers you can practise on. This course will not ask you to buy a phone or a laptop.

If something will not turn on at all, check the charger or power cable first, then ask a person who looks after that machine. This course is not a repair service.

sections.title: Shared words: screen, Settings, and apps

blocks.html:
Most devices share a few ideas, even when the brand is different.

The screen shows what is happening. You give commands by tapping (phone or tablet), clicking (mouse or trackpad), or typing (keyboard). Settings is the place where you change things such as volume, brightness, language, or Wi-Fi. On many phones it looks like a gear. On an iPhone, Apple’s help says you open the Settings app and can search for a word such as “volume.” On a Windows computer, Microsoft says you can open Settings by right-clicking Start and choosing Settings, or by pressing the Windows logo key and the letter I. Then you can search or browse categories.

Apps (on a phone or tablet) or programs (on a computer) are tools you open to do a job: mail, maps, a camera, or a web browser. Skills for Success names common digital tools and says to choose a tool that matches your task. This course stays with everyday device skills. It does not teach Word, Excel, or Outlook — those have their own LearnHere courses.

Menus look different on a Samsung phone, a Google Pixel, an iPhone, a Windows PC, or a Mac. When a lesson shows a practice screen, it is a drawing, not your exact device. If you cannot find a button, use the search box inside Settings, or ask a tutor. Google’s own Android help repeats that some steps vary by device.

sections.title: Why lock and update matter later

blocks.html:
A device is useful because it holds your information. That is also why later lessons spend time on locking the screen, careful Wi-Fi, updates, and passwords. Get Cyber Safe notes that phones and tablets hold a lot of information about us, and that computers and laptops do too — photos, contacts, and financial information among other things. You do not need to become a security expert. You only need a few calm habits: lock the screen when you step away, think before you join an unknown network, and say yes to updates when the device asks.

Skills for Success also includes safe, responsible practices: protecting personal information, knowing what you can and cannot share, and being careful with online risks. This course introduces those habits in everyday language. It is not a full privacy-law course. When a later lesson talks about scams or strange messages, it will stay short and point you to *Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada* for more depth.

For now, the goal is simpler: know what you are holding (a computer, a tablet, or a phone), know that Settings is where many controls live, and know that a library machine counts as a real place to learn. Write down any new word — screen, Settings, app, or lock — and ask a tutor if a label on your device does not match this lesson. Learning the names first makes the click-paths in later lessons easier to follow.

lessons.title: Power on, lock the screen, and find Settings

sections.title: Turn the device on and wait

blocks.html:
Press the power button until the screen lights up, then wait. The first screen may ask you to swipe, enter a PIN or password, or use a fingerprint or face if that option is already set up. On a Windows computer, Microsoft describes signing in with a password, a PIN, or Windows Hello (a fingerprint or face) if those are set up. Choose your account if more than one appears, then enter the sign-in you already use. If you forget a password or PIN, Microsoft’s sign-in screen can include a link to reset it — ask a tutor before you try a reset on a shared machine.

On a phone, waking the screen is not the same as unlocking it. After the screen lights up you still need the lock you have chosen, unless the phone was set to stay unlocked. Google’s Android help says a setting of None or Swipe gives no protection: anyone who picks up the phone can open it. If the device belongs to a library or council, use only the practice account staff give you. Do not try other people’s accounts.

If nothing happens when you press power, check that a charger or power cable is connected. Then ask for help. Forcing extra buttons at random can make a shared computer harder for the next person to use.

Once you are in, pause and look at the screen. You do not need to open every app today. The next step is to know where Settings lives, and how to lock the device when you stand up.

sections.title: Find Settings and review the screen lock

blocks.html:
Settings is the control room. On many Android phones, Google’s steps for a screen lock start there: open the Settings app, tap Security (if you do not see Security, Google says to check your phone maker’s help), then tap Screen lock. If a lock is already set, you must enter it before you can pick a different one. Then choose the option you want and follow the on-screen steps. Google lists PIN (four or more numbers, with a six-digit PIN recommended), Pattern, or Password (four or more letters or numbers — Google calls a strong password the most secure of these options). None and Swipe, again, give no protection.

On an iPhone, Apple’s help says to open Settings and then, depending on the model, tap Face ID & Passcode or Touch ID & Passcode, then Turn Passcode On or Change Passcode. You can view passcode options there. To change how soon the iPhone locks itself, Apple lists Settings > Display & Brightness > Auto-Lock, then a length of time.

On Windows, Microsoft says you can lock a computer that is already signed in by pressing the Windows logo key + L, or by opening Start, choosing the power icon, and choosing Lock. Locking keeps your apps and files open in the background. Anyone who wants to use the computer after that must sign in again. That is different from signing out, which closes your session and can lose unsaved work.

This course will never ask you to type your real PIN or password into a practice screen. If you change a lock on your own phone, do it on the real device, with a tutor nearby if you want company, and store the new lock only in your memory or a safe password manager — not on a sticky note.

sections.title: Lock when you step away

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe says to give a computer a strong log-in password and to lock it when you are not around. For phones and tablets, it says to use a lock-screen password and to turn on extra lock options, such as a fingerprint, if they are available. It also says to turn on auto-lock so the device locks after a short time. Even at home, locking the screen helps keep photos, messages, and files private.

Get Cyber Safe also says never to write a password down and then store it near the computer, and never to share your password with anyone. Their passphrase page repeats that last point in plain language: never share your passwords with anyone. A note stuck to the screen helps the next person as much as it helps you — and that is the problem.

If you only leave for a minute, lock anyway. On Windows, Windows key + L is a fast path that does not close your work. On a phone, use the power button to turn the screen off so auto-lock can do its job. If you share a device with family, each person should use their own sign-in when the machine allows it. Microsoft describes switching users so one person does not have to close everything for another — useful at home, less common on a locked-down library PC.

If you get locked out of your own phone because you forgot the passcode, official help exists (Apple describes steps if an iPhone is disabled). Do not guess over and over on someone else’s device. Ask the owner or staff.

lessons.title: Touch, click, type, and scroll with care

sections.title: Tap, hold, and type on a phone

blocks.html:
A touch screen waits for a clear, calm touch. Google’s Android help says: to select or start something, tap it. To type, tap where you want to type and an on-screen keyboard appears. In some apps you can touch and hold text to see more actions, such as when you play a song.

Apple describes the same idea with five basic iPhone gestures. A tap is a brief touch with one finger — for example, to open an app on the Home Screen. Touch and hold means you press an item until something happens (Apple’s example: touch and hold the wallpaper until the app icons begin to jiggle). You do not need every extra menu today. If icons start to jiggle and you did not mean to move them, tap Done or press the Home button if your phone has one, or ask a tutor — do not keep poking at random.

Type slowly at first. The on-screen keyboard may show letters, numbers, and a key that looks like a globe or a 123 key to switch layouts. If a letter does not appear, you may have tapped slightly beside the key. Delete with the backspace key (often an arrow pointing left). On a shared phone, do not type passwords or bank details as “practice.” This lesson only asks you to type a word such as your first name in a notes app you already use, or in a box a tutor points to.

If the screen does not respond well, Google also describes a Display & touch setting called Touch sensitivity on some Android phones (Increased sensitivity makes the screen more responsive to lighter touches). That is useful if you use a screen protector, but it is optional. Skip it unless a tutor helps you look.

sections.title: Swipe, scroll, zoom, and find Home or Back

blocks.html:
Swipe means you move one finger across the screen quickly. Apple’s example is swiping left on the Home Screen to see more apps. Scroll is slower: you move one finger without lifting it, such as dragging a list up or down in Photos. Apple says you can swipe to scroll quickly, then touch the screen to stop. Zoom uses two fingers: spread them apart to zoom in, or move them together to zoom out. Google says that on some pages, such as a webpage or map, you can also tap twice to zoom in, or pinch open and closed.

Getting around the phone uses either buttons or gestures. Google says steps vary by device and maker. On many Android phones you can choose:

  • 3-button navigation: dedicated buttons for Home, Back, and Recents (Overview). Google recommends this if you have limited dexterity or find precise gestures hard.
  • Gesture navigation: swipe instead of buttons. To go Home, swipe up from the bottom. To go Back, swipe from the left or right edge (from the far edge if the app also scrolls sideways). To see recent apps, swipe up from the bottom, hold, then let go. From there you can tap an app to reopen it, or swipe up on an app image to close it.

You can go Back more than once, but when you reach the Home screen you cannot go back any further. On an iPhone without a Home button, Apple’s separate gesture list (not copied here in full) uses a swipe up from the bottom to go Home.

A useful extra: Google says you can swipe down from the top to open Quick Settings, then find a tile such as Auto-rotate. Two fingers swiping down opens the full Quick Settings on many phones. That is the same “swipe down” idea as opening an Internet panel, which you will use again when you connect to Wi-Fi.

sections.title: Click, type, and switch windows on a computer

blocks.html:
On a computer, a mouse or trackpad moves a pointer (often an arrow) around the screen. Microsoft describes keyboard shortcuts as another way to do something you would typically do with a mouse. You do not need to memorise a long list. A few official shortcuts are enough for everyday work:

  • Windows logo key + E opens File Explorer (you will use this in the next lesson).
  • Windows logo key + L locks the computer (Lesson 2).
  • Windows logo key + I opens Settings.
  • Alt + Tab switches between open windows.
  • Alt + F4 closes the active window. If no windows are open, Microsoft says this can prompt you to shut down — so use it only on a window you mean to close.
  • Esc stops or leaves the current task, or dismisses a dialog box.
  • Ctrl + C copies the selected item; Ctrl + V pastes it; Ctrl + X cuts it.
  • Arrow keys, Page Up, and Page Down move through text or a page.

Microsoft’s File Explorer help also describes right-click or press and hold for more options on an item, and the shortcut list includes Shift + F10 to display the shortcut menu for a selected item. That menu is useful when you want to rename, copy, or see more choices. On a library computer, open only items staff say you may use.

Type on the physical keyboard the same way you would type a note: click or tap in the box first so a cursor (a blinking line) appears, then type. If letters show up in the wrong place, click in the box again. The Backspace key deletes characters to the left of the cursor; Delete removes characters to the right.

Take care with shared machines. A strong click is not better than a gentle one. If the pointer disappears, move the mouse; if the screen is dark, wake it the way you learned in Lesson 2 rather than hammering keys.

lessons.title: Files, folders, and finding what you saved

sections.title: What a file is, and what a folder is

blocks.html:
A file is one saved item: a photo, a note, a recording, or a webpage you downloaded. A folder is a container that holds files (and sometimes other folders). Think of a paper folder in a filing cabinet: the folder is not the letter; it is the place you put the letter so you can find it later.

On a Windows computer, Microsoft describes File Explorer as the tool that helps you find, open, organize, and manage files and folders on your PC (and, if you use it, in the cloud). The well-known folders Microsoft lists are Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Music, and Videos. In recent Windows 11 versions those folders are pinned in Quick access (also called File Explorer Home) and in the left navigation pane. Downloads is often where a file lands when you save something from a browser. Documents is a calm place for notes and letters you write yourself.

A file also has a name. A name you will recognise next week (“april-rent-receipt” or “practice-note”) is more useful than “Document1.” Microsoft’s File Explorer help includes a way to show file name extensions (View > Show > File name extensions on Windows 11). An extension such as .txt or .jpg is a short tag at the end of the name. You do not need to change extensions in this course. Just notice them if they appear.

You do not have to keep every file forever. Deleting something you do not need can make a list easier to scan — but on a shared or library computer, delete only files you created in this practice, and ask first. Google’s Android help for finding files similarly says you can delete a file to Trash from the Files app. Trash means it may not be gone forever right away, but you should still treat delete as a serious step.

sections.title: Open File Explorer and look in a known folder

blocks.html:
To open File Explorer in Windows 11, Microsoft says to select it on the taskbar or the Start menu, or press the Windows logo key + E. The same three paths appear in Microsoft’s Windows 10 notes on that page. (As of 10 November 2026, that page also states that support for Windows 10 ended on 14 October 2025. That date is written here so you know why a library machine might look different; it is not a quiz fact.)

Once File Explorer is open you will usually see Home (Quick access) first. Look down the left side for Documents or Downloads. If the left pane is hidden, Microsoft’s steps are View > Show > Navigation pane. If someone unpinned the known folders, Microsoft describes how to show them again: open File Explorer, select Home, select the Up arrow beside the address bar to see all six known folders, then right-click (or press and hold) a folder and choose Pin to Quick access.

To move a file, Microsoft says: select it, choose Cut on the ribbon, go to the new location, then choose Paste. For items sitting in Quick access you may need to right-click (or press and hold) and choose Open before you can cut and paste. The right-click menu also shows Cut, Copy, Paste, Rename, Share, and Delete along the top — hover to see each name. Those are the everyday actions. You do not need cloud search or OneDrive to practise today.

Search is useful when you remember part of a name. Microsoft says you can search from File Explorer Home to find relevant files on the PC (and in the cloud if you have signed in). Type a word from the file name and wait for the list to update. If nothing appears, check that you are looking in the right folder, or try a shorter word.

On a library PC, stay inside the folders staff point you to. Do not open other people’s documents.

blocks.html:
On many Android phones, Google says you can usually find your files in the Files app. If you cannot find that app, the phone maker may have given it another name — Google says to check the maker’s help. Open the Files app and you will see categories. Tap a category, then tap a file to open it. You can sort by name, date, or size (More > Sort by). To share a file, touch and hold it, then tap Share. Extra actions such as printing or adding a file to Google Drive sit behind More after you open the file.

Music, movies, or books you downloaded inside another app may live in that app, not in Files. Google’s example is videos downloaded in a movies app: go back to the app where you downloaded them. If you connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable, Google says to open the computer’s Downloads folder to find files that are on the device. Ask a tutor before you plug a personal phone into a shared computer.

The habit that saves the most time is a clear name at the moment you save. When a notes app or a browser asks “Save as,” type a short name that includes what the file is and, if you want, a month. Avoid spaces-only names or a string of numbers you will not remember. Then, later, search for one word from that name in File Explorer or in the Files app.

Skills for Success includes managing and storing digital information as part of everyday digital skill. You do not need a perfect filing system. One or two folders you understand — for example Documents on a PC, or a clearly named folder a tutor helps you create — are enough to start.

lessons.title: Connect to Wi-Fi without giving away too much

sections.title: Join a network you already know

blocks.html:
Wi-Fi is a wireless way to reach the internet through a nearby network. On many Android phones, Google’s steps (some of them only on Android 12 and up) are: open Settings, tap Network & internet, then Internet, then tap a listed network. Networks that need a password show a lock icon. After you connect, the network is “Saved,” and when you are nearby with Wi-Fi on, the phone can join it again automatically.

Google also describes a faster path: swipe down from the top of the screen, tap Internet, and select a network in the panel that appears. You can use that panel to switch networks quickly. To disconnect, Google’s path is Settings > Network & internet > Internet, then the Wi-Fi settings beside the connected network, then Disconnect. To forget a saved network, touch and hold it and tap Forget — useful if you joined the wrong name.

On Windows 11, Microsoft’s steps are: select the Network, Sound, or Battery icons on the taskbar to open quick settings; on the Wi-Fi quick setting, select Manage Wi-Fi connections; choose the network and select Connect; type the network password, then select Next. If you do not see the name you expect, Microsoft says you can refresh the network list. On Windows 10, the same Microsoft page says: select the Network icon on the taskbar (or the Up arrow if the icon is hidden), choose the network, select Connect, type the password, then Next, then Yes or No when asked whether the PC should be discoverable.

This course will never ask you to type a real Wi-Fi password into a practice screen. If you connect on a real device, type the key only in the real prompt, with a tutor nearby if you want company.

sections.title: Read the name, and read the lock

blocks.html:
The most important check happens before you type anything: is this the network you meant to join? Names can look alike. “TownLibrary” and “TownLibrary_Free” are not automatically the same network. Get Cyber Safe says cyber criminals sometimes create fake or “evil twin” hotspots that sit in the same place or use a similar name to lure people. When you can, ask someone from the organisation that hosts the Wi-Fi for the real name before you connect.

A lock icon (on Android, Google says this marks a network that requires a password) is not the same as “this network is safe.” It only means you need a key to join. A café can have a lock and still be a public network that many people share. An open network with no lock is even easier for anyone nearby to join.

After you connect, Android can save the network and rejoin it later. That is handy at home. It is less handy if you saved a network you did not mean to trust. Forgetting the network (touch and hold, then Forget) clears that automatic join. On Windows, Microsoft also describes saved (“known”) networks in Settings.

If a device asks whether it should be discoverable (Windows 10’s Yes or No question), treat a public place as a place where you usually do not want other people’s devices to find yours. When you are unsure, ask a tutor rather than tapping Yes out of habit.

Keep the “before you connect” checklist nearby. It is a short list you can reuse in a library, a hall, or a café.

sections.title: Public Wi-Fi is convenient, not private

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe says public Wi-Fi is flexible and can save mobile data, but unsecure public networks are not the safest option because anyone can connect — including people who might try to harm you. On the same network, someone may try to reach your device or listen in on traffic. They can also try to spread malware, especially to devices that are not kept up to date. That is one reason Lesson 6 spends time on updates.

Fake hotspots are the name-alike problem from Chapter 2. Ask staff for the official network name. If you are in a public Wi-Fi zone but you do not need the internet, Get Cyber Safe says to turn Wi-Fi off. Never use public Wi-Fi to open a bank account page or to make a purchase. If you use public Wi-Fi often, Get Cyber Safe says a virtual private network (VPN) can be a safer extra: it sends your traffic through a separate encrypted path. They note that many internet providers offer a VPN as a secondary service. This course does not recommend a brand.

Two more everyday habits: watch for shoulder surfers (people reading your screen), and prefer sites that protect the page itself. Get Cyber Safe says not to trust the wireless encryption on a public network alone. Look for a padlock icon at the start of the address bar. Many browsers, they note, no longer show the words HTTP, HTTPS, or www. The padlock is the sign to look for. You will practise that idea again in Lesson 7.

None of this is legal advice, and it is not a promise that a network is safe. It is a short list of official Canadian precautions so you can use Wi-Fi with fewer surprises.

sections.title: An account is a name the device knows

blocks.html:
An account is a sign-in that belongs to you (or to a library practice user): an email address plus a secret, or a phone number plus a code. Google Play’s help notes that apps and other content are connected to your Google Account, not only to one phone — and that you cannot move purchases between different accounts. Apple’s App Store steps ask you to confirm a download with Face ID, Touch ID, or your Apple Account password. Those are good reasons to treat an account as something personal.

This course will never ask you to type a real account password, PIN, or payment card into a practice screen. If a tutor wants you to practise signing in, use a practice account they give you, on the real device, not inside this lesson. On a shared computer, sign out when you finish if staff ask you to, so the next person does not land in your mail.

Skills for Success includes using digital tools and following safe, responsible practices with personal information. A simple habit is enough for today: know which account you are using before you install an app or say yes to a purchase. Google Play warns that if you have more than one account on a device, you should be signed in to the account you intend to use before you complete a purchase. If you buy something on the wrong account, they say to contact the app developer about a possible refund — this course cannot do that for you.

If a screen suddenly asks for a password when you did not tap Sign in, pause. Lesson 9 covers that kind of surprise. For now, close the unexpected box or ask a tutor rather than typing.

sections.title: Get apps from the official store

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe says to download apps from the App Store or Google Play and to review the permissions an app asks for. That is the everyday rule. A random link in a message is not an official store.

On many Android phones, Google’s Play Store help says: open the Google Play Store app (or go to play.google.com in a browser), search or browse, select the item, then select Install or the item’s price and follow the on-screen steps. Some content is free; some you pay for. Google also notes that apps are meant for supported Android and Chromebook devices and cannot be used on Windows or Mac computers. After you install, you can find the app on a Home screen or in the full app list (Lesson 3).

On an iPhone or iPad, Apple’s help (page published 22 October 2026; opened 10 November 2026) says: open the App Store, browse the Today, Games, Apps, or Arcade tabs or use Search, then tap Get or the price. If you see Open instead, you already have that app. Confirm with Face ID, Touch ID, or your Apple Account password. Apple says a Get button means the app is free to download — you will not be charged for that download — but some free apps offer in-app purchases and subscriptions later. Read those screens before you tap.

Permissions are the extra things an app wants, such as the camera or your location. Get Cyber Safe asks you to review them. If an app that is only a flashlight asks for your contacts, ask a tutor before you allow it. You can usually change permissions later in Settings, but the details differ by phone.

sections.title: Say yes to updates

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe’s software-updates fact sheet says the best and easiest way to protect devices that hold personal information is to update software regularly. Many people think updates are only for new features or bug fixes. Get Cyber Safe says that is not the whole story: updates often include new security features. Ignoring them can leave a device more open to malware and other attacks. They suggest turning on automatic updates, and running updates when you have a quiet moment. Look for updates on operating systems, antivirus software, web browsers, games, and apps.

On Windows, Microsoft’s steps (opened 10 November 2026) are: Start > Settings > Windows Update, then Check for Windows updates. If updates are waiting, choose Download & install, and restart if you are asked. On Windows 10, the same page lists Start > Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update, then Check for Windows updates. That page also states that support for Windows 10 ended on 14 October 2025 — a date-stamped fact, not a quiz item. A library PC may still show Windows 10; follow staff rules rather than trying to upgrade a machine that is not yours.

On many Android phones, Google says you will get a notification when an update is available. You can also open Settings, tap System, then Software updates, and follow the on-screen steps. Google advises connecting to Wi-Fi and charging to at least 75% before a large update. Update timing varies by device, manufacturer, and mobile carrier. To update apps, Google Play’s help says: open Play Store, tap your profile icon, tap Manage apps & device, then See details under Updates available, and tap Update or Update all. Some app updates ask you to accept new permissions.

On an iPhone or iPad, Apple’s wireless path (page published 15 September 2026; opened 10 November 2026) is: back up first, plug into power, join Wi-Fi, then Settings > General > Software Update. If an update is waiting, tap Download and Install. Apple says keeping software up to date is one of the most important security steps, and automatic updates can download and install overnight while the device charges on Wi-Fi.

Do not install an “update” that arrives as a surprise pop-up in a browser or a text message. Use Settings or the official store instead.

lessons.title: Browsers, search, and deciding if a page is trustworthy

sections.title: A browser is a window onto the web

blocks.html:
A browser is the program you use to look at websites: Chrome, Edge, Safari, or another app your device already has. You do not need to install a new one for this lesson. Skills for Success describes Digital skill as including finding, managing, and evaluating information — which is what you do when you search and then decide whether a page is the one you wanted.

To search, open the browser and type into the search box or the address bar. Google’s Search help says you can start with a simple query, then add more descriptive words if you need them. If you want a place or a service in a certain town, add the place name (their example style is a bakery plus a city). Choose words that are likely to appear on the page you want. Google also notes that spelling is usually corrected for you, and that capital letters do not change the search.

You can search for weather, a definition (add the word *define* in front of a term), a simple calculation, or a unit conversion. Those shortcuts are handy. They are not a replacement for reading the page you land on. If several results appear, look at the name of the site and the short description before you tap. A council page, a provincial page, or a well-known organisation is often a calmer starting point than the first colourful ad.

This lesson will not teach you to install extra search tools or to change a library computer’s default browser. Use what is already there.

sections.title: Look at the address, then look at the security status

blocks.html:
After you open a page, look at the address bar at the top. Get Cyber Safe says many popular browsers, including Chrome and Safari, no longer display the words HTTP, HTTPS, or www. They tell people to look instead for a padlock icon at the start of the address field as a sign that the site is using a more secure connection. They also say not to rely on public Wi-Fi encryption alone.

Chrome’s own help (opened 10 November 2026) describes the idea in its own words: Chrome changes the icon next to the site address when a site may be unsafe. On a computer, you check the security status symbol to the left of the web address. Chrome names three kinds of status: Default (Secure), Info or Not secure, and Not secure or Dangerous. You can select the icon for a summary of privacy details and page information. On an Android phone, Chrome’s steps are: open the page, tap More, then Site controls, and check the same kinds of status. If Chrome’s “Always use secure connections” setting is on, a site that does not support HTTPS can show a warning that the connection is not secure.

The picture on your screen may not match an older memory of a padlock. Follow the words you can actually see — especially Not secure or Dangerous — and ask a tutor if the icon is new to you. A “secure connection” means the browser has set up a protected link to that address. It does not prove that the organisation is honest or that the page is the one you intended. A look-alike address can still show a secure connection.

If you did not mean to visit a site, use Back (Lesson 3) rather than typing private information.

sections.title: Does this page match what you asked for?

blocks.html:
A secure-looking connection is only one check. The next check is identity: is this the organisation you thought it was?

Get Cyber Safe’s passphrase page says legitimate websites will never ask you to send personal information or to log in through an email or a text message. If you are unsure about a message, they say to log in from the home page of the organisation you are dealing with — and never to click a link in a suspicious message or reply to a message that asks for your password. That habit belongs here as well as in the longer *Email & Online Safety* course: type a known address yourself, or search for the organisation’s name and open the official result, rather than following a surprise link.

Look at the address character by character if something feels off. A missing letter, an extra word, or a different ending can mean you are not where you thought. Search results can include ads and look-alike names. Prefer a result that clearly belongs to a government, a library, a bank you already use, or another organisation you recognise — and still check the address after it opens.

Skills for Success includes evaluating information and being careful with online risks. You do not need to become an investigator. If a page asks for a password, a card number, or SIN-type information and you did not go looking for that page yourself, stop and ask someone. This course is not legal or fraud advice; it is a pause-and-check habit.

lessons.title: Everyday email and messages on a phone or a computer

sections.title: Texts, chat apps, and email

blocks.html:
People send short notes in more than one way.

A text (SMS) uses a phone number and the Messages app that came with many phones. A chat or messaging app (the name differs by brand) sends notes over the internet once you have an account. Email uses an email address and a mail app or a website such as Gmail. Skills for Success names email as one of the everyday digital tools people use to communicate. This lesson stays with those everyday moves. It does not replace *Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada*, and it does not teach Outlook — that course covers workplace inbox habits.

Each channel has a place. A text is handy for “I am at the desk.” Email is better when you want a subject line, a longer note, or a record you can search later. Get Cyber Safe says not to use text messages to send personal or sensitive information, and to avoid sending sensitive information by SMS or email when you are dealing with unexpected messages. If a note contains a health detail, a password, or banking information, stop and ask whether you should use a more private method — or wait and speak to the person.

On a shared or library computer, open only a mail account staff say you may use (often a practice account). Sign out when you finish if they ask you to. Do not open someone else’s inbox to “have a look.”

sections.title: Write a short message you mean to send

blocks.html:
The labels differ by app, but the idea is the same: say who the note is for, what it is about, write the words, then send.

Gmail’s official write-and-send help (opened 10 November 2026) describes one common computer path: go to Gmail, click Compose at the top left, add recipients in the To field, add a subject, write your message, and click Send at the bottom. Drafts are saved automatically in a label named Drafts. You can also add Cc or Bcc recipients if you need copies. Other mail apps use different button names, but a tutor can point to the same four parts: who, subject, message, send.

Keep a first practice note short and plain. For this course, write to a tutor or to a practice address staff give you — not to a real employer, bank, or government office. Say who you are, why you are writing, and what you would like the person to know. You do not need fancy formatting. You do not need to attach a file today.

If you attach something later, remember Get Cyber Safe’s warning about surprise files (Chapter 3). On the sending side, attach only a file you created and that the other person expects. Double-check the To field before you tap Send so the note does not go to the wrong person. If your app offers Undo send for a few seconds, that can rescue a slip — Gmail describes an Undo option after sending — but do not count on it.

sections.title: Think before you tap a link or an attachment

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe explains that phishing can arrive as email, as a phone call, or as smishing (a text). The best everyday defence they list is to stay alert: never respond to unexpected messages from unknown numbers, avoid sending sensitive information by SMS or email, and think twice before clicking links or opening attachments.

Their “think before you text” list is specific:

  • Do not use texts to send personal or sensitive information.
  • Never open attachments from unknown or untrusted sources.
  • Never click the links or call the phone numbers in suspicious messages — even if they say they are from your bank or mobile provider.

Malware can also reach a phone through internet downloads, text attachments, or Bluetooth transfers, Get Cyber Safe notes. That is one more reason to skip a surprise file and to turn Bluetooth off when you are not using it (their phones-and-tablets page asks you to do that so other people cannot try to pair with your device).

If a message looks urgent (“your account will close today”), that urgency is a reason to slow down, not to hurry. Use the habit from Lesson 7: open the organisation from its real home page or a saved bookmark if you still need to check something. The longer safety course has more examples of scams. This lesson only asks you to treat unexpected links, attachments, and phone numbers as things you can ignore until you have asked a person you trust.

sections.title: A passphrase is a longer secret you can remember

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe calls a password the key to your personal information, and says unique, complex passphrases and passwords for every account and device are one of the best protections you have. They recommend a passphrase when you can use one: a memorized phrase of mixed words, with or without spaces. Their recipe is a combination of four or more random words and a minimum of 15 characters. Random words are harder to guess than a pet’s name or a birthday.

If a site will not accept a passphrase, they describe a traditional password instead:

  • at least twelve characters
  • upper- and lower-case letters and at least one number
  • at least one character that is not a letter or number, such as !, #, or $
  • a series of letters that only make sense to you, such as the first letters of each word in a sentence

Do not invent a passphrase out loud in a public room, and do not type a real one into this course. Practise the *shape* of the idea (four random words, long enough) with words that are not your real secret. If you change a real password later, do it on the real sign-in page of the service, after you opened that page yourself.

A PIN is a shorter number used to unlock a device (Lesson 2). It is not a replacement for a unique password on an email or banking account. Google’s Android help, from Lesson 2, recommends a six-digit PIN if you choose PIN for the screen lock, and lists a strong password as the most secure of those lock types.

sections.title: Unique secrets, stored safely

blocks.html:
Many people reuse the same password everywhere. Get Cyber Safe says the problem is simple: if a criminal gets into one account, they can try that same secret on the others. Unique passwords are the easiest way to protect all of your accounts after one service has a breach. They also mention that you can try a password manager if remembering many secrets is hard. This course does not name or sell a brand.

Get Cyber Safe repeats, clearly: never share your password with anyone. Their laptops page also says not to write a password down and store it near the computer. A note on the monitor, a photo of a password, or a text that says “my password is…” hands the key to whoever picks up the device.

If you must write a hint while you are learning, keep it away from the device and make it a hint only you understand — or, better, use a password manager a tutor can help you choose later. Do not store real passwords in this course, in email drafts, or in a shared notes file on a library PC. A family member can help you remember *that you have an account*, but Get Cyber Safe is clear that they should not be given the password itself.

Signing in from a trusted place matters as much as the secret itself. The next chapter covers messages that try to collect a password you already created.

sections.title: Messages that try to collect a password

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe describes phishing (email) and smishing (text) as messages that pretend to come from someone you trust so you will give up information. To get a password, a phishing email may look like a well-known company and ask you to log in or send you to a fake sign-in page.

Their rule is direct: legitimate websites will never ask you to send personal information or to log in through email or text. If you are unsure, log in from the home page of the organisation you are dealing with. Never click a link in a suspicious message, and never respond to a message that asks for your password.

That overlaps Lesson 7 and Lesson 8 on purpose. The extra point here is the password itself: even a strong, unique passphrase is worthless if you type it into the wrong box. Open the real site yourself (type a known address, use a bookmark, or search for the organisation’s name and check the result). If a pop-up or a text creates urgency, treat the urgency as a warning.

For a wider set of scam examples, tone, and reporting tips, use *Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada*. This lesson will not retell that course. If a message still worries you after you have paused, show it to a tutor rather than guessing. You can ignore an unexpected note; you cannot easily take back a password once you have typed it in the wrong place.

lessons.title: When something goes wrong — simple checks and who to ask

sections.title: Start with the simple checks

blocks.html:
When a device “does not work,” the cause is often something small. This course is not a tech-support contract and it will not walk you through a force-restart on a shared phone — those steps differ by model, and guessing at buttons can make things worse. Try this calm list first.

  1. Power. Is a charger or power cable connected? A dark screen may mean an empty battery, not a broken computer. If nothing happens after you connect power and press the power button once, stop and ask for help.
  2. Wake and lock. Press the power button or a key to wake the screen. If you see a lock screen, sign in the way you already do (Lesson 2). On Windows, Windows key + L locks the computer without closing your work; signing in again should bring that work back.
  3. Volume and sound. If a video or call seems silent, look for a volume key or a volume control in Settings rather than tapping at random.
  4. Internet. If a page will not load, check whether Wi-Fi is on and whether you joined the network you meant (Lesson 5). Get Cyber Safe says you can turn Wi-Fi off when you do not need it — so it may be off on purpose.
  5. Settings and search. Open Settings (Lesson 1 and 2) and search for the word you need, such as volume or Wi-Fi, instead of browsing every menu.

If the screen is frozen, do not keep pressing keys harder. On Windows, Microsoft lists Ctrl + Alt + Delete as a way to open a security screen where you can lock, switch user, sign out, or open other tools. Ask a tutor before you sign out of a shared machine, because unsaved work can be lost. On a phone, ask staff rather than holding unfamiliar button combinations.

sections.title: Who to ask, and what to do if a device is missing

blocks.html:
You are not expected to fix everything yourself. Good people to ask:

  • A tutor or library staff member, for a machine in that building.
  • A family member you already trust, for a home device — without handing them every password (Lesson 9: never share your password).
  • Your phone or internet service provider, for a lost phone or a network that will not come back after the simple checks.
  • Local police, if a device is stolen.

Get Cyber Safe says you should never leave a phone in a vehicle or unattended in public, and you should keep a record of the make and model. If the device goes missing, their steps are:

  1. Contact your service provider. They can help deactivate the device and restore it to factory settings, and they can place the phone on a national blacklist so it will not work on any Canadian wireless network.
  2. Report it to local law enforcement. If you can find the device’s coordinates, give that information to the authorities. Never attempt to recover stolen property by yourself.

Those steps are safety information, not legal advice. This course cannot blacklist a phone for you and cannot contact police for you.

Be careful about “help” that appears on the screen without you asking: a pop-up that names a phone number, a person in a café who offers to “fix it if you unlock it,” or a message that asks for remote access. Use the people and numbers you already know, or that staff give you.

sections.title: Put the everyday skills on one list

blocks.html:
You now have a short set of habits that work on a phone and on a computer:

  • Name the device and find Settings (Lesson 1).
  • Power on, lock the screen, and use auto-lock (Lesson 2).
  • Tap, scroll, go Home or Back, and use a few Windows shortcuts (Lesson 3).
  • Find a file in File Explorer or the Files app, and save with a clear name (Lesson 4).
  • Join a known Wi-Fi network and treat public Wi-Fi with care (Lesson 5).
  • Use official app stores and say yes to updates (Lesson 6).
  • Search, then check the address and the security status (Lesson 7).
  • Send a plain practice message, and skip surprise links or attachments (Lesson 8).
  • Use a strong, unique passphrase and never share it (Lesson 9).

The capstone below asks you to try five of those skills on a real device, with staff nearby for Wi-Fi. You do not have to be fast. You do not have to own a new phone. A library or council computer still counts. If a brand’s labels differ from a practice screen, ask — screens differ, and this course said that from the first page.

When you finish the capstone, take the final exam. It is multiple choice, it is the only graded piece, and the pass mark is 70 percent. You have two attempts. The certificate is a sample of completion; it is not college credit and not a tech-support licence.

assignment.title: Everyday-skills checklist (capstone)
assignment.html: Try these five skills on a real device you are allowed to use. A library or council computer counts. Ask staff to stand nearby before you join Wi-Fi. Do not type a real password, PIN, or Wi-Fi key into this course — only into the real device, if you need to.

Find a file you saved, or save a short practice note with a clear name and find it again
Connect to a known Wi-Fi network with staff nearby (skip this step if staff ask you not to change the network)

assignment.answerKey: There is no single numeric answer. You should be able to say, in your own words, how you locked the screen, where the file lives, which network name staff confirmed, what you noticed in the address bar, and who received the practice message. Tick “I tried this” when you have done the steps you are allowed to do.
